newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Prospect grows of early decision on EMU rates.
newsitem.headline: Prospect grows of early decision on EMU rates.

text.p: The prospect of an early accord on how European currencies will be fixed to a single currency grew on Thursday after EU monetary commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said the issue might be reviewed later this year.

Speculation about a decision on the method by which national currencies will be converted to the euro arose earlier this week after the Financial Times said Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean Claude Juncker would push for an early accord.
Luxembourg takes over the EU presidency in July until December.
Speaking at a news conference de Silguy, pressed to respond to the Luxembourg plan, said the European Commission might have a look at the issue later this year.
"We may have something to say (on exchange rates) during the Luxembourg presidency," de Silguy said.

EU monetary officials say the decision, one of the most important outstanding hurdles ahead of the decision on which countries qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU), has not been formally discussed among the relevant EU bodies, although informal talks may have been initiated.

The EU's monetary committee, comprised of national treasury and central bank officials, may have its first chance to tackle the issue in September, ahead of an informal meeting of finance ministers and central bankers in Luxembourg, officials said.

While it is impossible to determine the conversion rates without knowing which countries will participate in EMU, there is a strong desire to clarify the "method" by which the rates will be "irrevocably" locked against the new currency.
The favoured approach at the moment, and perhaps most politically expedient, is to use the existing central parity rates in Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).

Since virtually all of the currencies in the grid are trading close to their central rates -- the one exception being the Irish punt -- there is a strong argument in favour of using them in the conversion to the euro.
"I think this is probably the cleanest and least controversial way to do it," said a senior EU official.

A second proposal, one floated by outgoing European Monetary Institute President Alexandre Lamfalussy, is to take an average of market rates over the last months or years up to the end of 1998 -- or just before the euro is launched on January 1, 1999.
The primary purpose behind coming up with an early decision on the methodology is to minimise market speculation ahead of the euro's introduction.
It is hoped that an early announcement will answer one of the markets' most pressing questions and thereby quell what could be a very turbulent transition period ahead of 1999.
